entry.title: Displaying Flexible Workflow Status Directly in SAP GUI for SD Documents
entry.content:
Introduction

Flexible Workflow in SAP S/4HANA supports approval processes for SD documents, but detailed workflow information is not always available where SAP GUI users perform their daily work.

This post shows how a lightweight open-source extension makes the current approval step and workflow history directly accessible in VA03. It also provides an overview of the technical approach used to integrate the information without creating additional workflow-status tables.

The problem

Many SD users still work mainly in SAP GUI.

The overall approval status is visible, but important details are not directly available in the SD document:

  • Who is currently responsible?

  • Which approval steps have already been completed?

  • Who approved or rejected the document?

  • When was the decision made?

  • Were any decision comments entered?

To access this information, users normally need to leave the SD document and open separate workflow applications or transactions.

The solution

The extension adds the Flexible Workflow information directly to VA03.

Users can view the current approval state and open the detailed workflow information without leaving the SAP GUI.
Figure 1: Flexible Workflow status displayed directly in the SD document in VA03.

The detailed view displays:

  • the approval history

  • current and previous processors

  • the status of each workflow step

  • timestamps

  • decision comments

Figure 2: Detailed workflow history including processors, step status, timestamps and decision comments.

This gives SAP GUI users direct access to the information they need while working with the SD document.

Technical approach

The solution reads the workflow information directly from SAP Business Workflow at runtime.

No custom workflow-status tables are used, which avoids duplicated data and additional synchronization logic.

The integration uses SAP enhancement options available for the SD document. An additional toolbar status button can be included, but it is optional and can be omitted if customers want to avoid further SAP GUI enhancements.

Open Source

The solution was created from a real requirement in daily SAP work.

Instead of turning this small enhancement into another licensed add-on, we decided to make it available as open source.

The project is published under the MIT license and can be installed using abapGit.

GitHub repository:

https://github.com/m2-digital-ch/abap-sd-flexible-workflow-gui

Conclusion

This extension closes a usability gap by making existing Flexible Workflow information directly accessible in VA03. Users can review the current approval step and the complete workflow history without switching away from the SD document.

The example also shows that a small, targeted enhancement can improve transparency for SAP GUI users without duplicating workflow data or changing the underlying approval process.

entry.title: C_TS462_EN_2601: Understanding the New System-Based Exam Pattern
entry.content:
The SAP Certified – Implementation Consultant for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, Sales certification has taken a slightly different approach with the new C_TS462_EN_2601 exam pattern.

I recently went through this new format, and one thing that stood out to me was the shift from a mainly question-based assessment to a more practical, system-based assessment. This changes the way we should prepare for the certification as well.

This blog is based on my personal experience with the exam and my preparation journey. The exam structure and content may change over time, so candidates should always refer to the latest information provided by SAP.

What is different in the new exam pattern?
The biggest difference is that you are required to work with the SAP system and achieve a specific outcome.

In my experience, the assessment consisted of around 5 to 6 practical task groups. Each task provided a high-level requirement along with the expected outcome. The task does not necessarily take you through every step that needs to be performed.

This means you need to understand the requirement first, identify the relevant configuration or process, perform the required activities in the system, and finally make sure that the expected result is achieved.

The overall approach can be thought of as:

Understand the Requirement → Perform the Configuration/Activity → Execute the Process → Validate the Expected Outcome

The system then validates whether the required outcome has been achieved.

This makes the exam feel much closer to a real implementation scenario. Instead of simply asking, "Which option is correct?", the assessment is more focused on "Can you actually make this work in the system?"

How does this change the preparation approach?
Because of this change, I would not recommend preparing only by reading theory or memorising questions.

The SAP Learning Journey available through SAP Learning Hub is a very good starting point. It provides structured learning across the important areas of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition Sales and helps build the conceptual foundation required for the certification.

But while going through the Learning Journey, I would strongly recommend spending time in an SAP system as well.

For example, when learning about pricing, don't stop after understanding pricing procedures and condition types. Try creating the relevant configuration, maintain the required master data, create a sales order and check how the pricing is determined. If the expected condition does not appear, try to understand why.

The same approach can be followed for sales documents, delivery, billing, availability checking and other areas.

This hands-on practice makes a big difference because SAP Sales is highly interconnected. A small configuration or master-data setting in one area can affect the outcome somewhere else.

Focus on understanding the process
One of the important things I realised during preparation was that understanding the relationship between different configuration areas is more useful than memorising individual steps.

For example, when working with a sales order, it is important to understand how the sales document type, item category, schedule line category, pricing, partner determination and availability checking work together.

Similarly, understanding the complete flow from:

Sales Order → Delivery → Post Goods Issue → Billing

helps you identify where a particular issue may be coming from.

The same applies to areas such as credit management, account determination, output determination, text determination and partner determination.

You don't necessarily need to memorise every configuration screen. You should be comfortable enough with the concepts to understand what needs to be configured, where it needs to be configured, and what impact it will have on the business process.

My preparation approach
For my preparation, the combination that worked best was:

SAP Learning Journey + Conceptual Understanding + Hands-on Practice

I used the Learning Journey to understand the concepts and then tried to connect those concepts with actual system activities.

I found it particularly useful to practise a topic immediately after learning it instead of leaving all the hands-on practice until the end.

Also, don't be afraid of troubleshooting during practice. If a configuration does not produce the expected result, try to find the reason instead of immediately checking the solution.

That troubleshooting experience is valuable because, in a real SAP implementation, things rarely work perfectly on the first attempt.

entry.title: Automatic FIFO Batch Determination & Batch Split in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (SD)
entry.content:
Automatic Batch Management: FIFO Batch Determination & Batch Split Configuration Guide — SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (SD Module)

Scope: Sales Org 1000 | Division 30 (LPG) | Distribution Channels 10–30 | Sales Document Type OR
Category: Logistics / Batch Management / Batch Determination for Sales and Distribution

Introduction

In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, standardizing business processes while adhering to the Clean-Core Principle is vital. A frequent requirement in the Sales and Distribution (SD) module under Batch Management is the automated picking of inventory based on FIFO (First-In, First-Out) logic during delivery creation, including an automatic Batch Split when the oldest available batch cannot fulfill the total item quantity.

Since traditional SPRO backend transactions are restricted in the Public Edition, this guide provides a step-by-step walkthrough of how to configure custom batch determination fields and strategies utilizing SSCUI (Self-Service Configuration UI) activities and Fiori applications under the Batch Determination for Sales and Distribution sub-node.

1. Business Requirement & Scope

The client requires that in the Outbound Delivery (OBD), as soon as the user manually selects a Storage Location for a material line item, the system should automatically propose batch(es) following a FIFO method. If the quantity available in the first (oldest) batch at that storage location is insufficient to cover the required delivery quantity, the system must automatically execute a Batch Split, pulling the remaining balance from the next sequential batch without demanding any manual batch entry from the warehouse operators.

  • Sales Organization: 1000
  • Distribution Channels: 10 to 30
  • Division: 30 (LPG products)
  • Sales Document Type: OR (Standard Order) — the delivery inherits this via the order type assignment

2. Configuration Objects Created — Summary

The table below represents the custom and standard objects deployed via Central Business Configuration (CBC) to achieve this division-wide automated layout:

Object Type

Technical ID

Purpose / Description

Condition Table

501

Plant / Storage Location / Material — for material-specific overrides if ever needed

Condition Table

502

Plant / Storage Location only — covers ALL materials at a location (used for this requirement)

Access Sequence

Z501

FIFO – Plant/SLoc/Material (Access 10 = Table 501, Access 20 = Table 502)

Sort Sequence

YB_FIFO_SORT

Standard SAP-delivered sort rule — sorts by Batch Number ascending (proxy for chronological FIFO)

Batch Class

YB_BATCH

Standard SAP-delivered Class Type 023 (Batch) — linked as Selection Class in the strategy type

Strategy Type

Z01

"FIFO-SLoc wise Auto" — links Access Sequence Z501, Sort Sequence YB_FIFO_SORT, Selection Class YB_BATCH, Batch Split enabled

Search Procedure

ZFIFOS

"FIFO Batch Determination-SLoc" — contains Strategy Type Z01 at Step 10

Assignment

1000/10/30/OR → ZFIFOS

Search Procedure assigned to Sales Org/Channel/Division/Document Type combination

 

3. Step-by-Step Configuration

Step 1: Material Master — Activate Batch Management

In the Manage Product Master Data Fiori App (or MM02), on the Sales: General/Plant view, the Batch Management (Plant) indicator must be activated for the relevant LPG materials.

Step 2: Material Master — Batch Classification (Class YB_BATCH)

The material must be assigned to the standard SAP batch class YB_BATCH ("Batch FIFO first-in-first-out"), Class Type 023, in the Classification view. This class carries the characteristics Batch Number, Vendor Batch Number, and Date of Last Goods Receipt, linking each individual batch asset to the search/selection logic.

Classification view of material 110000000 (LPG) — Class YB_BATCH assigned with characteristic values

Step 3: Condition Tables — 501 and 502

Two SD condition tables need to be maintained under the SSCUI node: "Create Condition Tables to Determine Batches for Sales and Distribution".
• Table 501: Plant / Storage Location / Material (For potential exceptions).
• Table 502: Plant / Storage Location only. This allows a clean blanket record to automatically cover every material at a given storage location without mapping materials individually.

General Business Data – Products – Batch - Batch Management - Batch Determination for Sales and Distribution - Create Condition Tables to Determine Batches for Sales and Distribution

SSCUI activity list — 'Create Condition Tables to Determine Batches for Sales and Distribution' highlighted

Step 4: Access Sequence Z501

A new custom access sequence Z501 ("FIFO – Plant/SLoc/Material") was created instead of modifying standard SD01 paths, protecting the clean-core guidelines.
• Access step 10: Points to Table 501.
• Access step 20: Points to Table 502 as the catch-all mapping.

Define Sales and Distribution Access Sequences' highlighted

Access Sequence list — custom Z501 created alongside standard profiles

Z501 Accesses detail — Step 10 & 20 assigned to Condition Tables 501 and 502

Step 5: Sort Sequence — YB_FIFO_SORT

Rather than building a custom sort routine, the standard SAP-delivered sort sequence YB_FIFO_SORT ("Sorting rule for batches FIFO") was used directly since it is already Released in Public Cloud.
It utilizes the characteristic YB_BATCH_NUMBER in Ascending order. Since the cloud environment numbers system-generated batches sequentially, sorting by ascending batch numbers acts as a perfect proxy for chronological FIFO execution.

Sort Sequence' screen — YB_FIFO_SORT identified as pre-delivered content

 

Display Sort Sequence YB_FIFO_SORT — Basic Data view confirming Released status

Display Sort Sequence YB_FIFO_SORT — Characteristics mapping with Ascending flag checked

 

Step 6: Strategy Type Z01

Strategy Type Z01 ("FIFO-SLoc wise Auto") was created under Application V (Sales/Distribution) with the following mandatory parameters:
• Access Sequence: Z501
• Selection: Class Type 023, Class YB_BATCH
• Sorting: Sort Sequence YB_FIFO_SORT
• Quantity proposal: Qty proposal = 1 (Top-Down Assignment). Leave Dialog batch determin. unticked so that the system automatically handles allocation in the background without disturbing the user with manual popup screens.

Define Sales and Distribution Strategy Types' node highlighted

Strategy Types list (Application V) for reference

Strategy Type Z01 — Initial field layout and assignments

Strategy Type Z01 — Saved configuration confirmation status

 

Step 7: Search Procedure ZFIFOS

Search Procedure ZFIFOS ("FIFO Batch Determination-SLoc") was created, and Strategy Type Z01 was assigned at Step 10 / Counter 1.

“Define Sales and Distribution Search Procedures” node highlighted

New Entries screen — Search Procedure ZFIFOS created

ZFIFOS Control Data — Step 10, Counter 1 mapped to Condition Type Z01

 

Step 8: Assign Search Procedure to Sales Area / Document Type

In the activity "Allocate SD Search Procedure/Activate Check", the matrix row containing Sales Org 1000 / Distribution Channel 10 / Division 30 / Document Type OR (along with channel rows 20 and 30) was updated to point to the new ZFIFOS procedure with Check Batch enabled.
This targeted assignment ensures only Division 30 LPG products trigger this specific logic, while all other divisions remain on standard mappings unaffected.

Technical Note: This configuration maps to the Sales Order type parameters (validated against table TVAK), not the delivery type (LF), since the execution timeline for batch resolution is triggered during the delivery phase via item category configuration controls.

“Allocate SD Search Procedure/Activate Check” node highlighted

 

Allocation screen — 1000/10/30/OR row updated to ZFIFOS with Check Batch activated

 

Step 9: Batch Search Strategy — Condition Records

Condition records were maintained via the Fiori app Manage Search Strategies – Sales and Distribution (the cloud functional equivalent of transaction VCH1).
By selecting Strategy Type Z01 and choosing the key combination Plant/Location (Table 502), blanket records were created for the target locations (Plant 1160 / SLoc SS01 and Plant 1150 / SLoc PP01–PP04). Leaving the material field blank ensures that every material managed at these storage locations automatically inherits the FIFO rules without individual master mapping.

Fiori Launchpad home screen navigating to “Manage Search Strategies”

Create Batch Search Strategy screen — Selecting Key Combination Plant/Location (Table 502)

 

Selection criteria entry screen for Plant 1160 and Storage Location SS01

Fast Entry screen — Condition record created for Plant 1160 / SLoc SS01

Fast Entry screen — Blanket condition records maintained for Plant 1150 / SLoc PP01–PP04

 

4. Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for the Warehouse Team

To successfully trigger the automated allocation and split during outbound logistics execution, operations teams should follow this sequence:

  1. Create or open the Outbound Delivery (OBD) document originating from the Standard Sales Order (OR).
  2. Navigate to the Picking tab layout.
  3. Manually populate the designated Storage Location (SLoc) field (e.g., SS01) for the material line item row.
  4. Click on the Batch Split action button located in the lower application toolbar, and then click Batch Determination.
  5. The system will instantaneously cross-reference available inventories in sequential order, assign the appropriate batch IDs, split the delivery line items cleanly to satisfy the open requirement, and fulfill the transaction smoothly without manual data entry.

Outbound Delivery screen — Entering SLoc SS01 and Click the Batch Split function

Item Detail view — Click the 'Batch Determination' function

Automated Execution — Quantities successfully split across batches 0000000260 and 0000000261 following FIFO rules

Conclusion

By leveraging standard SAP-delivered selection components combined with custom condition assignments, we achieved smooth background multi-batch fulfillment in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. This approach aligns with cloud-compliance frameworks while completely eliminating operational friction on the warehouse floor.

entry.title: Inbound IDoc Custom Fields Converted to Uppercase Despite Lowercase Configuration
entry.content:
We enhanced a standard inbound IDoc with custom header and item fields. During inbound processing, lowercase values received in the IDoc are being converted to uppercase before updating the application tables. One field uses CHAR20 without a domain, while another uses a lowercase-enabled domain. Looking for guidance on whether this is standard SAP behavior, a data element/domain issue, or a product limitation.

Body

Background

We recently enhanced a standard Inbound IDoc by introducing custom fields at both header and item levels.

Header Field

  • Segment Field: E1EDK01-ZZAAS_INDICATOR
  • Data Element: Based on predefined type CHAR20
  • No custom domain assigned

Item Field

  • Segment Field: E1EDP01-ORD_ITEM_06-ZZOFFER_TYPE
  • Data Element uses a custom domain
  • Domain is configured with Lowercase Allowed

Our business requirement is to preserve the exact case of the values received in the inbound IDoc.

Observed Behavior

The inbound IDoc contains lowercase values, but during processing the values are converted to uppercase before being saved to the application tables.

Values Received in IDoc

 
E1EDK01-ZZAAS_INDICATOR = aas indicator
 
E1EDP01-ORD_ITEM_06-ZZOFFER_TYPE = pct1
 
Values Stored After Inbound Processing
 
 
E1EDK01-ZZAAS_INDICATOR = AAS INDICATOR
 
E1EDP01-ORD_ITEM_06-ZZOFFER_TYPE = PCT1
 
This behavior is observed even for the field whose domain has the Lowercase indicator enabled.

Analysis Performed

  • Verified that the custom domain for ZZOFFER_TYPE has the Lowercase checkbox enabled.
  • Confirmed that no conversion exit is assigned to the domain.
  • Verified that the inbound IDoc payload contains the values in lowercase.
  • Observed that the values are converted to uppercase during inbound processing before being persisted.

Questions for the Community

  1. Is there any standard SAP inbound IDoc processing logic that automatically converts custom character fields to uppercase?
  2. Should the Lowercase Allowed setting on the domain be sufficient to preserve the case during inbound processing?
  3. Does using a predefined CHAR20 data element without a dedicated domain cause SAP to force uppercase values?

entry.title: Confluent's New AI Engine Meets SAP: What Changes
entry.content:
Confluent's Real-Time Context Engine reached general availability in May 2026. The premise is clean: instead of an AI agent querying your source systems, or waiting on a batch job, it materializes Kafka topics into a low latency serving layer and exposes them to agents over Model Context Protocol. You enable it on a topic, point an agent at an endpoint, and the agent can read your data.

For anyone who has fought to get SAP data out of the system and into something an application can use, this sounds like the last mile finally getting solved.

I spent a few time testing it against a real SAP table to find out what actually changes. The short version: getting the data to the agent is solved. Getting the agent to understand it is not, and one of the failures is worse than not answering at all.

The setup

One topic, carrying VBAK exactly as it comes out of SAP. Not a curated extract, not a renamed view. The sales document header table, with its real structure, streamed into Confluent Cloud with an Avro schema in Schema Registry.

Three sales orders in it, posted across September, plus one junk record that a test data generator dropped in. I left the junk in on purpose.

Then the Real-Time Context Engine enabled on that topic, and an agent connected over MCP

How the data got there, and why it matters to the argument

The capture side deserves a paragraph, because the whole point of this exercise is what happens when data is genuinely current rather than merely recent.

The topic is fed by application layer business events thanks to OneConnect by Onibex. When a sales document is created or changed in SAP ECC or S/4HANA, the application raises an event, and that event is pushed outbound over an HTTP RFC destination of type G to a gateway, which streams it to Kafka with a registered schema. Nothing polls the database. Nothing runs a delta extractor on a schedule. The update is triggered by the transaction, which matters because a schedule does not know when anything happened. It only knows what time it is.

The implementation here is Onibex One Connect, which I work on. I name it because it is the one whose internals I can describe accurately rather than approximate, and because the capture mechanism is load bearing for the rest of this post. The evaluation questions at the end are the part worth taking away, and they apply whatever produces your topics.

The consequence is that the record the agent reads is the record SAP posted, as of the posting. Not last night's close, not a fifteen minute window. That is the property everyone is chasing, and it is the property that turns the rest of this post from a curiosity into a risk.

The topic list, with the Real-Time Context Engine column on the right.

The engine exposes exactly three tools to the agent: listTopics to discover what exists, getMetadata to read a schema, and queryData to run a read only SQL query against one topic.

What the agent sees

Before anything else, it is worth looking at what getMetadata returns for VBAK, because that is the agent's entire understanding of your data.

One hundred nineteen columns. The names are SAP's, with no descriptions attached. Nine fields called TAXK1 through TAXK9. Five called KVGR1 through KVGR5. KNKLI is the credit control account, CTLPC is the risk category, AMTBL is the released amount, and nothing in the schema says so.

Every date field arrives as VARCHAR: ERDAT, AUDAT, ANGDT, BNDDT, GWLDT, BSTDK, MAHDT, AEDAT. That is faithful to SAP, where DATS is a character type. It is also the root of two of the four problems below.

And no key is declared. Every field is nullable, VBELN included. The only field with a type of its own is the Kafka record key, which is opaque bytes.

What works

A lot, and it is worth being fair about this before the criticism.

Asked for the sales orders, the agent discovered the topic, read the schema, queried it, and came back with a clean table. It recognized the junk record on its own, separated it out, and suggested purging it before the topic feeds anything downstream. That is genuinely good behavior and it took about four seconds.

Three orders and one junk record, discovered and separated without being told.

Filters, ranges, compound predicates and ORDER BY all work. Latency is not the story. The serving problem really is solved.

Where it breaks, in four steps

One: what works by accident.

Filtering a date range works:

WHERE "AUDAT" >= '20260901' AND "AUDAT" <= '20260905'

It returned the right orders. But AUDAT is a string, and this worked only because SAP's DATS format is YYYYMMDD, which happens to sort the same as text and as a date. Point the same engine at a field formatted DD.MM.YYYY and the identical query returns wrong rows with no error at all.

Two: what is refused outright.

SELECT SUM("NETWR") FROM "Oneconnectdemo_VBAK"
QE_UNSUPPORTED_AGGREGATION
"GROUP BY and aggregation functions are not supported."

This is documented and deliberate. No aggregates, no GROUP BY, no joins, no subqueries.

Three: what cannot be expressed at all.

WHERE TO_DATE("AUDAT", 'yyyyMMdd') >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30' DAY
FE_SQL_NOT_SUPPORTED
"Unsupported SQL feature: Function 'TO_DATE' is not supported."

There is no date conversion. Which means "show me the orders from the last thirty days" cannot be formulated against a raw SAP table. That is not an exotic request. It is close to the most common question a sales manager asks.

Four: what fails silently, and this is the one to worry about.

Ask for the orders of customer 1000123. That is how the number appears in an email, on a purchase order, in a conversation.

WHERE "KUNNR" = '1000123'
{"status":"success", "data":[]}

Zero rows. Status success. No error.

With SAP's leading zeros:

WHERE "KUNNR" = '0001000123'

 The order is there.

The first three failures announce themselves. This one answers calmly that the customer has no orders, and the person asking has no way to know the answer is false. Leading zero padding on CHAR fields is exactly the kind of knowledge that lives in an SAP consultant's head and in a data product definition, and that a table extract leaves behind. The agent is not guessing badly. It is guessing reasonably.

The failure I did not expect

Here is where it stops being a list of limitations and becomes something else.

The engine refuses aggregation. Beyond that, the MCP server injects an instruction into the model at connection time. The text is worth quoting exactly:

> "If the user asks for an unsupported operation (aggregation, JOINs, mutations), explain the limitation clearly instead of attempting it. Do not work around unsupported operations by fetching raw data and computing results manually."

So the guardrail exists, and the instruction not to route around it exists.

I asked the agent for the total value of all the sales orders.

It queried the topic. It pulled the rows. It added them up itself. Then, finding one order in USD and two in MXN, it searched the web, took a USD to MXN rate from a financial data site, converted, and returned a single figure: 2,789,118.25 MXN.

The arithmetic is correct. The number is meaningless.

It is meaningless because SAP would not value that order at a market rate pulled from a website. It would use the exchange rate type stored in KURST on the document, against the rate table, on the document's date. The figure the agent produced does not exist in any SAP report, and it never will.

To the agent's credit, it said so, in a line at the bottom that most people will skip: SAP would value that order at the rate type in KURST, so the books may show a different figure.

That caveat is the difference between a careful agent and a reckless one. It is not the difference between a right answer and a wrong one. The number at the top of the response still looks like a fact.

What this actually tells us

The Real-Time Context Engine does what it says. Data reaches the agent in milliseconds, with role based access control and audit logging, without the agent touching the source system. As a serving layer it is solid, and the architecture behind it is sound.

What it does not do, and does not claim to do, is make the data mean anything.

Every one of the four failures above is a semantic failure, not a performance failure. A date stored as text is not a date. A customer number is not a customer number until you know the padding convention. An amount is not comparable to another amount until someone decides which exchange rate applies. None of that is in the schema, so none of it reaches the agent, so the agent fills the gap with the most reasonable assumption available. Sometimes that assumption is right. Sometimes it returns empty. Sometimes it goes to the internet and invents a number.

The uncomfortable part is that real time makes it worse, and this is the argument I did not expect to be making.

A nightly extract is obviously stale, and people treat it accordingly. Nobody commits a credit decision to a number they know is twelve hours old without checking. That skepticism is a safety mechanism, and it is accidental: it exists because the data was slow, not because anybody designed it.

Take the delay away and the skepticism goes with it. An answer that arrives in four seconds, formatted as a table, drawn from an event the ERP raised a moment ago, carries an authority that its semantics have not earned. The pipeline is right about when. It is silent about what. And the freshness is what makes people stop asking.

So the work that real time capture saves you at the transport layer, it hands straight back at the semantic layer, with interest. Getting the event out of SAP the instant it happens is the part that is solved. Making sure the thing that arrives means what a business user thinks it means is the part that is not, and shipping the first without the second is how you build a system that is confidently wrong at speed.

Where this leaves the work

The fix is not a faster engine. It is upstream, in whatever produces the topic.

Publish AUDAT as a date type rather than a character string, and the thirty day question becomes expressible. Normalize the padding on KUNNR when the record is produced, and the customer lookup stops silently failing. Resolve the currency conversion once, in the pipeline, using the rate type on the document, and publish the converted amount as a field. Then the agent is not converting anything, because the answer is already a column.

That is what a declared contract does. It moves the knowledge out of the consumer's assumptions and into the definition, where a functional consultant can review it and disagree with it before an agent ever sees it.

And it costs nothing in freshness, which is the part worth being explicit about. Typing a date, normalizing a padded field and resolving a currency are declarations, not batch steps. They are decided once, when the data product is defined, and applied to each event as it passes. The stream does not slow down because somebody wrote down what AUDAT is. What streams is that declaration made live, which is a very different thing from a pipeline that happens to be fast.

For anyone evaluating this: the question to ask is not how fast the context arrives. It is what your agent will assume about every field where your schema is silent, and whether you would be comfortable with that assumption appearing in a number somebody acts on.

What this test does not cover

This ran against one table, in a demo environment, with four records. I did not measure throughput or latency under load, and no figure here should be read as a benchmark.

I tested a single agent. A different model, or one given a system prompt that enforces the tool's constraints more firmly, might refuse the aggregation instead of computing it. The server side instruction is the same for everyone; how strictly a model honors it is not something I can generalize from one run.

The engine is currently AWS only, requires a registered schema on the topic, and its upsert mode requires the record key in raw byte format rather than a registry format. That last constraint is worth checking against how your topics are produced before you plan around it.

Josue Ramirez is a Data and AI Engineer at Onibex, working on SAP streaming integration and semantic layers for ERP data.

entry.title: Consolidated Invoice getting split due to Credit Account change in Business Partner
entry.content:
Introduction
    Open sales orders can be created over a period of time, if in between the Credit Account is updated in the Business Partner, then the new orders created after the change will carry the new Credit Account, whereas the orders created before the change will continue to have the old Credit Account or blank. When a consolidated invoice is created for such orders, system splits the invoice instead of combining them, since the Credit Account is a header relevant field for billing.

    How to correct the Credit Account on existing open orders
    SAP provides standard program UKM_RFDKLI20 to update the Credit Account/Credit Segment on open sales orders, based on the current credit data maintained in Business Partner.

    This program updates open orders only for one Business Partner at a time, in case Credit Account is changed for multiple Business Partners, program needs to be executed separately for each Business Partner.

    To avoid this manual effort, we can build a custom program to identify all such Business Partners and update the orders automatically.

    Development

    Step1: Identify Business Partners with Credit Account change.
    Change documents CDHDR and CDPOS are read for object class BUPA_UKM, table UKMBP_CMS and field LIMIT_RULE, filtering on the values that represent a Credit Account/Credit Profile change. This identifies the Business Partners where Credit Account/Credit Profile has changed on a given date/time.

    SELECT objectid, changenr FROM cdhdr
INTO TABLE lt_cdhdr
WHERE objectclas = 'BUPA_UKM' AND udate      = sy_date.

SELECT objectid, changenr FROM cdpos
INTO TABLE lt_cdpos
FOR ALL ENTRIES IN lt_cdhdr
WHERE changenr  = lt_cdhdr-changenr
    AND tabname   = 'UKMBP_CMS'
    AND fname     = 'LIMIT_RULE'
    AND value_new = 'STANDARD'.

    Step2: Business Partners identified in Step1 are mapped to the corresponding Customer number in program UKM_RFDKLI20. Run the program using loop for all the customers to update the Credit Account on all their open orders.

    This program can be scheduled as a background job at regular intervals or at the end of the business day, so that open orders are always updated with the latest Credit Account, and consolidated invoice does not split due to this reason.

    LOOP AT lt_final INTO ls_final.

  " Normalize BP number to Customer number (KUNNR)
  lv_kunnr = |{ ls_final-objectid+0(10) ALPHA = IN }|.

  IF lv_kunnr IS NOT INITIAL.
    APPEND VALUE #( sign = 'I' option = 'EQ'
                     low = |{ lv_kunnr ALPHA = OUT }| ) TO s_cust.

    " Run standard program for this customer
    SUBMIT ukm_rfdkli20
           WITH pkunnr IN s_cust
           WITH sdchd = 'X'          " create SD change documents
           WITH testlauf = ' '       " live run
           AND RETURN.
  ENDIF.

ENDLOOP.

    Conclusion: This blog explains the issue of consolidated invoices getting split due to Credit Account change in Business Partner, and how it can be corrected and automated using program UKM_RFDKLI20.

entry.title: Adding New Text Fields: Text Determination Configuration Guide for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
entry.content:
Adding New Text Fields: Text Determination Configuration Guide for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (SD Module)

Scope: Text Determination for SD Documents | Example: Outbound Delivery Header (Text Object VBBK, Procedure T6)

Category: Logistics / Sales and Distribution / Text Determination Configuration

Introduction

In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, keeping business processes standardized while staying within the Clean Core principle really matters. A common requirement in the Sales and Distribution module is adding extra text fields, at header or item level, on documents such as Sales Orders, Outbound Deliveries and Billing Documents, so that teams like Sales, Logistics or Finance can record information that the standard text types simply do not cover.

Since traditional SPRO backend access is restricted in the Public Edition, this guide walks through how to add new text fields using SSCUI (Self Service Configuration UI) activities only. As a practical example, we add two new text fields to the Outbound Delivery header, but the same approach works for other documents and levels too. No custom fields, no Adapt UI changes, and no development work are needed for this.

  1. Business Requirement & Scope

For our example, the Logistics and Transport team needed two extra text fields at the Outbound Delivery header level, so that Vehicle Number and Cartage Contractor details could be captured directly on the delivery document, without a separate Z table or a custom field. This information is used purely for reference and tracking as the document moves through the process.

  • Text Object: VBBK (SD Document Header)
  • New Text Types: ZX01 (Vehicle No.) and ZX02 (Cartage Contractor)
  • Text Determination Procedure: T6 (Delivery Header)
  • Applicable documents: Outbound Delivery, for all delivery types that use procedure T6 (used here as the example document)

  1. Configuration Objects Created

The table below lists the objects created and maintained through SSCUI activities in Manage Your Solution to achieve this requirement.

Object Type

Technical ID

Purpose / Description

Text Type

ZX01

Vehicle No., new text type used to capture the vehicle number on the delivery header

Text Type

ZX02

Cartage Contractor, new text type used to capture the contractor details on the delivery header

Access Sequence

9000

Access sequence linked to the Vehicle No. text ID

Access Sequence

9001

Access sequence linked to the Cartage Contractor text ID

Text Determination Procedure

T6

Delivery Header procedure, both new text IDs assigned here at sequence 20 and 25

 

  1. Step-by-Step Configuration

Step 1: Define New Text Types (SSCUI 105684)

Go to Manage Your Solution and search for 105684. Open the activity Define Text Types for SD Document Header. This activity works on text object VBBK, which covers the SD document header.

SSCUI search result for activity 105684, Define Text Types for SD Document Header

SSCUI search result for activity 105684, Define Text Types for SD Document Header

Add two new entries here, ZX01 for Vehicle No. and ZX02 for Cartage Contractor.

New text type entries ZX01 (Vehicle No.) and ZX02 (Cartage Contractor) added under text object VBBK

Step 2: Set Up Text Determination for the Delivery Header (SSCUI 101291)

Next, go back to Manage Your Solution and search for 101291, Set Up Text Determination for Delivery Header.

SSCUI search result for activity 101291, Set Up Text Determination for Delivery Header

Inside this activity, select procedure T6, Delivery Header, and then click Text IDs in Procedure in the dialog structure on the left.

Text Determination Procedures screen, T6 Delivery Header selected

Step 3: Assign the New Text IDs to Procedure T6

Enter the new text ID entries under T6. ZX01 is placed at sequence 20 and ZX02 at sequence 25, both set as Text Is Not Mandatory, and linked to access sequences 9000 and 9001 respectively.

Text IDs in Procedure T6, entries ZX01 and ZX02 added

Step 4: Create the Access Sequences

From the same dialog structure, click Access Sequences and add the new entries, 9000 for Vehicle No. and 9001 for Cartage Contractor.

Access Sequences list, 9000 and 9001 created for the new text IDs

Step 5: Maintain Access Sequence for Text IDs

Click Access Sequence for Text IDs and, for sequence 9000, add an entry pointing to text object VBBK (Sales: Header texts), ID ZX01, with All Languages checked. Repeat the same for sequence 9001, this time pointing to ID ZX02.

Access Sequence 9000 detail, mapped to text ID ZX01 (Vehicle No.)

Access Sequence 9001 detail, mapped to text ID ZX02 (Cartage Contractor)

Save the configuration once both access sequences are maintained.

  1. Verification on the Outbound Delivery

Once both SSCUI activities are saved, the new fields are ready to use. Here is how to check them:

  1. Open or create an Outbound Delivery, using the Create Outbound Delivery or Change Outbound Delivery app.
  2. Go to Header Details and select the Texts tab.
  3. The two new text types, Vehicle No. and Cartage Contractor, now appear in the list along with the standard text types.
  4. Select either one and enter free text, exactly like any other header text.

Outbound Delivery header, Texts tab, before the configuration

Outbound Delivery header, Texts tab, after the configuration, Vehicle No. and Cartage Contractor now available

  1. Adding More Text Fields or Using the Same Approach for Other Documents

Everything above was done for the Outbound Delivery header, but nothing in the approach is specific to it. Text determination works the same way across SD documents, so you can repeat it whenever a new text field is needed. Here are the most common cases:

  • More fields on the same document: repeat Steps 1 to 5 with a new text ID (for example ZX03), a new sequence number in procedure T6 and a new access sequence.
  • Other header texts, such as Sales Order or Billing Document: use the text determination activity for that document and select the matching value in the Group for field on the Text Determination Procedures screen. The rest of the flow stays the same.
  • Item level texts: work with the item text object and the item text determination procedure instead, then follow the same pattern of text type, procedure entry, access sequence and mapping.
  • Assigning the procedure to the right document types: use the Text Procedure Assignment node in the dialog structure, so that the document types you want actually pick up the procedure.

A few practical tips: keep new text IDs and access sequences in the customer namespace (for example Z prefixed text IDs and 9000 and 9001 for access sequences as used here), decide upfront whether a text should be mandatory using the Text Is Mandatory setting, and always confirm the result in the app before moving the configuration further. The exact SSCUI activity names can differ by document, so search for them in Manage Your Solution using the document name.

Conclusion

In this guide we created two new header text types (ZX01 Vehicle No. and ZX02 Cartage Contractor) under text object VBBK, assigned them to the Delivery Header procedure T6 with their own access sequences (9000 and 9001), and confirmed on the Outbound Delivery that both fields now appear in the Texts tab and accept free text. All of this was done with standard SSCUI activities only, so the Clean Core approach stays intact. If a new text does not show up on your document, check that the text ID is saved in the procedure, that the access sequence points to the correct text object and ID, and that the procedure is assigned to the document type you are testing. The same pattern can be repeated for more fields or for other SD documents.

entry.title: SD Credit Management: 5-Level Approval Workflow for Credit-Blocked Sales Orders
entry.content:
In SAP Sales and Distribution, credit management helps control customer exposure by checking the customer's credit limit when a Sales Order is created.

In a customer implementation, I worked on a requirement where a Sales Order should still be saved when the credit limit is exceeded, but it should be credit blocked for delivery until the required business approval is completed. To address this, we implemented a 5-level workflow-based Credit Management approval process.

Business Requirement

Sales Order → Credit Check → Credit Block → Approval Workflow → Credit Block Release → Delivery

When the customer's credit exposure exceeded the available credit limit:

  • The Sales Order must be saved successfully.
  • The Sales Order must be placed under credit block.
  • A workflow must be triggered automatically.
  • The required approval level must be determined dynamically.
  • Approvals must be routed sequentially from L1 to L5.
  • After the final approval, the credit block must be automatically released.
  • If rejected, the Sales Order must remain blocked.

How the Approval Level Is Determined

The approval level was not fixed for every Sales Order. It was determined using:

Company Code + Credit Limit Exhausted Value

The Credit Limit Exhausted value was calculated as:

Credit Limit Exhausted = Sales Order Net Value − (Credit Limit − Credit Exposure)

For example:

ParameterValue
Credit Limit1,000,000
Existing Credit Exposure900,000
Sales Order Value250,000
Available Credit100,000
Credit Limit Exhausted150,000

The calculated value is then compared with the customer's DoA (Delegation of Authority) matrix to determine the required approval level.

For example:

Credit Limit ExhaustedApproval
0 – 25,000L1
25,001 – 100,000L2
100,001 – 250,000L3
250,001 – 500,000L4
> 500,000L5

The above ranges are illustrative. Actual thresholds are maintained based on the customer's Finance/Credit Management DoA matrix. 

Technical Approach

The workflow is triggered when the Sales Order is saved and the standard credit check results in a credit block. The implementation checks:

KNA1-KTOKD = 'XD01'
VBAK-CMGST = 'B'

The Sales Order number is then passed to the workflow. Before triggering a new workflow, the system checks whether an active workflow already exists for the same Sales Order. The required information is retrieved from SAP Credit Management and Sales Order data, including:

Sales Order Net ValueVBAK-NETWR
Credit Control AreaVBAK-KKBER
Credit SegmentUKM_KKBER2SGM
Business PartnerVBPA
Credit LimitUKMBP_CMS_SGM
Credit ExposureUKM_COMMTS_READ

The calculated Credit Limit Exhausted value is then used to determine the applicable approval level.

Approval Workflow

The approval follows a sequential process:

Sales Order
↓
Credit Limit Exceeded
↓
Credit Block
↓
Calculate Credit Limit Exhausted
↓
Determine DoA Level
↓
L1 → L2 → L3 → L4 → L5 Approvals
↓
Release Credit Block
↓
Delivery

Each approver receives the blocked Sales Order in the workflow inbox. If an approver rejects the request, the Sales Order remains blocked. The exact rejection and resubmission behaviour can be defined based on the customer's business process. After the final approval, the workflow automatically updates the credit status and releases the Sales Order from the credit block.

This implementation demonstrates how standard SAP Credit Management can be combined with SAP SD and workflow capabilities to handle credit-limit exceptions in a controlled manner. Instead of simply rejecting a Sales Order when the credit limit is exceeded, the order can be saved, credit blocked, routed through the appropriate approval hierarchy, and automatically released after the required approval.

This approach provides a flexible and traceable solution for customer-specific credit approval requirements in SAP S/4HANA.

Testing and Challenges Faced

During testing, one of the important things to check was whether the workflow was triggered only when the Sales Order was credit blocked. Since users can save the same order multiple times, we also had to consider the possibility of duplicate workflow instances being created for the same Sales Order. To avoid this, the system checks whether an active workflow already exists before triggering a new one.

Another scenario to consider was a change in the Sales Order after approval. For example, if the order value increases after the approval is completed, the previously approved amount may no longer be sufficient. In such cases, the credit limit exhausted value needs to be recalculated, and the approval level must be determined again if the change affects the approval requirement.

Partial deliveries also need attention. Even if a Sales Order has been approved, the system should continue to follow the configured credit-check rules for subsequent delivery processing. The workflow approval should not automatically bypass any further credit checks required by the business.

These scenarios highlighted the importance of checking not only whether the workflow works correctly, but also whether the credit status remains consistent throughout the Sales Order process.

What I Would Improve

One thing I would focus on is keeping the approval-level determination separate from the workflow logic. Since the approval level depends on the company code and the credit limit exhausted value, maintaining the DoA thresholds in a configurable table would make future changes easier.

I would also give more attention to Sales Order changes after approval. Recalculating the exhausted value before releasing the credit block helps ensure that the approval is still valid for the current order. This is particularly important when the order value or the customer's credit exposure changes while the workflow is in progress.

Conclusion

Implementing this requirement helped demonstrate how SAP Credit Management and SAP Business Workflow can work together to handle credit-limit exceptions. Instead of preventing users from saving a Sales Order when the credit limit is exceeded, the order can be saved and kept blocked until the required approval is completed.

The main advantage of the five-level approval process is that the approval authority is determined based on the actual credit limit exhausted value rather than following the same approval route for every order. Although this requires additional workflow logic and testing, it provides better control over credit exposure and supports the customer's DoA requirements.

Before implementing a similar solution, it is important to define the approval thresholds clearly and consider scenarios such as order changes, partial deliveries, rejection, and changes in credit exposure. These details help ensure that the credit block is released only when the required business conditions are satisfied.

entry.title: Understanding SAP S/4HANA Order-to-Cash (O2C): From Sales Order to Billing
entry.content:
SAP S/4HANA Order-to-Cash: My Practical Journey Through SAP SD Configuration

Introduction

The Order-to-Cash (O2C) process in SAP S/4HANA connects customer orders with delivery and billing. While learning SAP Sales and Distribution (SD), I worked through the configuration of organizational structure and several sales and shipping components required for this process.

Rather than looking at each configuration setting separately, I wanted to understand how the different components fit together. My practice involved setting up a company code, Sales Organization, Distribution Channels, Divisions, Plants, Storage Locations, Shipping Points, Shipping Conditions, Loading Groups, and sales document controls.

In this blog, I will share my practical learning experience, explain the relationships between these components, and discuss a configuration dependency I encountered while setting up shipping point assignments.

Note: The organizational codes and business names used in this article belong to my Beretta practice scenario and do not represent a production client implementation.

1. Building the Enterprise Structure

The first part of my practice was setting up the organizational structure that supports sales activities.

I created the company and company code, defined the Sales Organization, and assigned the Sales Organization to the company code.

The main organizational values in my practice setup were:

   

Organizational ComponentCode
CompanyZBER
Company CodeZB01
Sales OrganizationB100
Distribution ChannelRT
Distribution ChannelON
DivisionFA
DivisionAM
DivisionPA

I then assigned the Distribution Channels and Divisions to the Sales Organization and configured the Sales Area combinations.

A Sales Area combines the Sales Organization, Distribution Channel, and Division. These assignments establish the organizational context for sales transactions.

This step helped me understand that creating organizational units is only part of the configuration. The required assignments must also be maintained so that these units can work together in the sales process.

2. Defining Plants and Storage Locations

The next part of my practice involved defining plants and assigning them to the company code.

I worked with the following plant structure:

   

PlantDescription
BF01Chennai Factory Beretta
BG01Chennai Beretta Godown
BS01Beretta Retail Shop 1
BS02Beretta Retail Shop 2

I also maintained Storage Locations to represent different inventory areas within the plants.

For example, BS01 and BS02 represented retail shop inventory, while the factory and godown had separate storage-location arrangements.

This helped me understand the difference between a Plant and a Storage Location. A plant represents a broader organizational location, while a storage location identifies an area within that plant where stock is managed.

The plant and storage-location structure is important because inventory management and goods movements depend on the relevant organizational assignments and stock data.

3. Configuring Shipping Points

After defining the plants, I worked on creating shipping points and assigning them to plants.

The shipping points in my practice setup were:

   

Shipping PointDescription
PORTChennai Port Terminal
AIRPChennai Airport
SHPCRetail Shop Chennai
SHPDRetail Shop Delhi

I also configured Shipping Conditions and Loading Groups.

     

ConfigurationCodeDescription
Shipping ConditionBABeretta Air Delivery
Shipping ConditionBSBeretta Ship Delivery
Shipping ConditionCPCustomer Pickup
Loading GroupZBBeretta Products

In standard SAP SD, Shipping Point Determination depends on the shipping condition, loading group, and delivering plant.

The shipping condition represents the relevant shipping arrangement, while the loading group is maintained in the material master and represents the material's loading requirements. The delivering plant identifies where the goods are supplied from.

These settings work together to determine the shipping point for delivery processing.

4. A Configuration Issue I Encountered and Resolved

One of the most useful lessons from my practice came while assigning shipping points to plants.

I had defined the plants and shipping points, but a particular plant was not appearing as expected during the shipping point assignment process. Initially, I was unable to proceed with the assignment.

After checking the prerequisite configuration, I identified that the assignment of the Sales Organization and Distribution Channel to the Plant had been missed. I corrected this assignment in the relevant configuration step using transaction OVX6.

After correcting the assignment, the plant appeared as expected in the shipping point assignment process, and I could proceed.

This experience helped me understand an important aspect of SAP configuration: creating an organizational object does not automatically establish all the relationships required for subsequent processing.

When an expected plant or organizational unit is missing, checking the prerequisite assignments can help identify the cause. In my case, correcting the missing assignment resolved the issue.

This was a useful learning experience because it showed me how configuration dependencies affect one another and why checking the assignments is just as important as creating the individual objects.

5. Configuring Sales Document Types and Item Categories

After working on the organizational and shipping configuration, I moved on to the controls used in sales document processing.

Sales Document Type

I defined the custom Sales Document Type ZBOR, used for the Beretta standard order in my practice setup.

The Sales Document Type controls important aspects of sales document processing, including the number range and other document-level settings.

Item Category

I defined the custom Item Category ZBTA for the Beretta standard item.

The Item Category controls how an individual item is processed in a sales document. Its configuration influences aspects such as pricing, delivery relevance, and billing relevance.

Schedule Line Category

I also defined the custom Schedule Line Category ZB for the Beretta line category.

Schedule Line Categories control settings at the schedule line level, including delivery relevance, availability checking, requirements transfer, and movement type where applicable.

Finally, I worked on assigning the Item Category to the Schedule Line Category through the relevant determination configuration.

These settings serve different purposes: the Sales Document Type controls the overall document, the Item Category controls the item, and the Schedule Line Category controls relevant delivery and inventory behaviour at the schedule line level.

6. Connecting Configuration to the O2C Process

The configuration steps above establish the organizational and processing framework needed for sales and shipping activities.

In a typical SAP SD process, a sales order records the customer's request. SAP uses the relevant organizational assignments, master data, and document controls to process the order.

The supplying plant is determined using the applicable master data and configuration. The shipping point is determined using the shipping condition, loading group, and delivering plant.

An outbound delivery is then used to manage shipping activities such as picking and packing. When Post Goods Issue (PGI) is successfully posted, inventory is updated and the relevant goods-movement and accounting documents are generated.

Billing follows according to the applicable billing process and creates the customer invoice.

The simplified document flow is:

Sales Order → Outbound Delivery → Post Goods Issue (PGI) → Billing

Each stage has a distinct purpose, but the stages are connected through document flow and configuration. Understanding these connections is essential to understanding the O2C process as a whole.

Conclusion

Working through the SAP SD configuration steps helped me understand how organizational structure, master data, and configuration assignments contribute to the Order-to-Cash process.

One important lesson was that configuration is not simply about creating individual objects. Their assignments and dependencies also matter. The issue I encountered while assigning shipping points was a practical example of this. After correcting the missing Sales Organization and Distribution Channel assignment to the Plant, the plant appeared as expected, allowing me to continue with the configuration.

This experience strengthened my understanding of how prerequisite assignments affect subsequent configuration steps.

The exact O2C process may vary depending on business requirements and the SAP system configuration. I plan to explore more SAP SD concepts and share additional learning experiences in future articles.

Thank you for reading!
